description: Hello! We are a team of juniors in our school’s STEM program. Currently, we specialize in using machine learning and local large language models. As dedicated researchers, we have a variety of experiences and resources that we can easily share with participants. We are looking for capable programmers to join our team. Specifically, we are looking for people who are adept at using local large language models, machine learning and training, and coding in JavaScript.
summary: FLARE (Flame in Freefall) is a static, keyless web app providing an evidence-grade fire-safety briefing on NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database of 1987-2025 (133 microgravity investigations, 24 Combustion Science), 2,572 publications, a ranked risk model on faceted experiment cards, and a knowledge graph. It is a response in kind to the three verbs of the brief. A corpus-wide data panel of PSI's own fields and per-investigation readings is summed into the app. Four-factor evidence rubric scoring ranks each question out of 100 on the factor that affects them (publication volume, safety coverage, flight status, recency). Explanations of matched terms, saying exactly how a result garnered a top ranking. TF-IDF/cosine semantic search on device provides an interactive display: about 9k identical text records, with comparison, and with inferred relationships (PSI: 18 links; FLARE: 90). No build, no API key, entirely in the browser, from a stamped PSI. Cyan is real NASA data, while violet is machine-read. Every claim has an accession number and DOI.
details:
FLARE (Flame in Freefall) is an interactive web application developed to enable exploration and application of NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database to the domain of spaceflight fire safety. A knowledge graph, a risk-ranking model, and searchable experiment cards categorize 133 microgravity investigations, including 24 in combustion science, and 2,572 publications spanning decades of research.

The application allows users to search research records using on-device semantic search, compare investigations side-by-side, and rank research findings based on four factors: publication volume, safety coverage, flight status, and recency. It also uses a local 125-billion-parameter LLM for SI analysis to identify and explain relationships between investigations, helping users understand existing research and identify potential gaps in knowledge.

The site takes existing NASA findings and makes them more accessible to fire-safety researchers and aerospace engineers. That helps them make evidence-based decisions before testing new fuels, materials, or fire-suppression systems in space. It aims to improve astronaut safety, reduce duplication of research, and guide future research in the directions where more work is needed.

The project was built with JavaScript, HTML, and CSS and deployed using GitHub Pages. It runs in the browser directly, using a local copy of the NASA PSI database, so there's no need for an API key or connection to an external database. The processing on the device also helps to keep accessibility and independence from external services.

FLARE is creative in that it combines semantic search, AI-assisted analysis, automated evidence ranking, and a knowledge graph into a single platform. Our team focused its research on accuracy, transparency, accessibility, and usability. We also developed the interface to distinguish original NASA information from machine-generated analysis, and claims were tied back to the original accession numbers and DOIs. This ensures the users are able to not only explore findings but also can check the evidence behind it.
